questions.prompt: Which part of an HTTP request says what the client wants to do with a resource?
questions.explanation: The method expresses the intended action. Host names the server; status codes and bodies belong to responses (requests can have bodies too, but they carry data, not the action).

questions.prompt: Which header tells the server which response formats the client can handle?
questions.explanation: Accept is for content negotiation of the response. Content-Type describes the body actually sent; Allow lists permitted methods.

questions.prompt: HTTP is stateless: each request must carry everything the server needs to process it, such as authentication.
questions.explanation: The protocol does not remember previous requests. Sessions are built on top with cookies or tokens sent on every request.

questions.prompt: Which method should you use to apply a partial update to a resource?
questions.explanation: PATCH applies partial modifications. PUT replaces the target resource's whole representation, POST is for processing/creating, and HEAD is GET without a body.

questions.prompt: What does this command show, and why is it useful to testers?
options: Only the response status line and headers, because HEAD returns no body; useful for checking headers and existence cheaply
An error, because HEAD is not a real method
questions.explanation: `curl -I` sends HEAD. The server returns the same headers a GET would, without the body, so you can check Content-Type, caching headers or status quickly.

questions.prompt: Which caching-related headers should a tester check on a GET for a public product catalogue? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Cache-Control sets the policy; ETag and Last-Modified enable conditional requests (304 Not Modified). Authorization is a request credential header, not a caching header.

questions.prompt: A GET with `If-None-Match: "v7"` returns 200 with the full body even though the resource's ETag is still "v7". What is the defect?
options: Conditional requests are not honoured: it should return 304 Not Modified with no body, wasting bandwidth otherwise
Nothing; 200 is always correct for GET
questions.explanation: When the ETag matches, the server should reply 304 so the client reuses its cache. 412 Precondition Failed is for If-Match failures on writes.

questions.prompt: Two testers update the same product. Tester 1 sends PUT with `If-Match: "v3"` after tester 2 already changed it to v4. What should a well-built API return?
options: 412 Precondition Failed, so the stale update does not overwrite tester 2's change
questions.explanation: If-Match gives optimistic concurrency control. A mismatched ETag means the client's view is stale; overwriting would silently lose an update.

coding.title: Parse a raw HTTP response
coding.prompt:
Write `parse_response(raw)` that parses a raw HTTP/1.1 response string (lines separated by `
`, a blank line before the body) into a dict `{'status': int, 'headers': dict, 'body': str}`. Header names must be lower-cased; values stripped.

Example: `parse_response('HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1}')` returns `{'status': 201, 'headers': {'content-type': 'application/json'}, 'body': '{"id":1}'}`.
coding.explanation: The first blank line separates head from body. The status line's second token is the code. Header names are case-insensitive, so lower-casing makes lookups reliable; partition on the first colon keeps values that contain colons (like URLs or times).
hints: The status code is the second word of the first line.
Use `partition(':')` so a value containing ':' is not cut.

tests.name: Status, headers, body
tests.code:
r = parse_response('HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1}')
assert r == {'status': 201, 'headers': {'content-type': 'application/json'}, 'body': '{"id":1}'}, r

tests.name: Header value with colons
tests.code:
r = parse_response('HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://x.test:8080/a

')
assert r['headers']['location'] == 'http://x.test:8080/a' and r['body'] == '' and r['status'] == 302

coding.title: Method properties table
coding.prompt:
Write `method_props(method)` returning a tuple `(safe, idempotent)` of booleans per RFC 9110 for GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE, POST, PATCH (case-insensitive). Raise `ValueError` for unknown methods.

Example: `method_props('put')` returns `(False, True)`.
coding.explanation: All safe methods are idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST and PATCH are neither (in general). Knowing this tells you which requests can be retried automatically.

tests.name: Safe methods
tests.code: assert method_props('GET') == (True, True) and method_props('options') == (True, True)

tests.name: Idempotent but unsafe
tests.code: assert method_props('put') == (False, True) and method_props('DELETE') == (False, True)

tests.name: Neither
tests.code: assert method_props('POST') == (False, False) and method_props('patch') == (False, False)

tests.name: Unknown raises
